packages.name: client
packages.doc:
Package client is the outbound half of the SDK's network domain (ADR 0029):
an HTTP client whose posture is enforced by the transport rather than by the
call site.

# Why the policy lives in the transport

A [Policy] is evaluated inside the http.RoundTripper, underneath every call
site. A caller cannot construct a request that skips it, because there is no
path to the network that does not pass through the transport. "This client is
read-only" therefore stops being a convention the next contributor has to
remember and becomes a property of the code — which is why [Client].HTTP can
safely hand the underlying *http.Client to a third-party SDK without
forfeiting the guarantee.

Every default is closed. A conjunction with no members refuses, a path
allowlist with no patterns refuses, and a client built with a nil policy is
refused outright. An allowlist that lost its contents — a renamed config key,
a slice never populated — must close, never quietly become a passthrough.

# Building a read-only client

	allow, err := client.AllowPaths(`/v1/(subscribers|supi/[^/]+|profiles(/[^/]+)?)`)
	deny, err := client.DenyPaths(`/v1/(authentication|policy|eir|oam).*`)
	policy := client.Policies(client.AllowMethods("GET"), deny, allow)

	c, err := client.New(client.Config{BaseURL: "https://sdm.core.svc:8000"},
		identity, policy, func(call client.CallInfo) {
			logger.Info(ctx, lg, "egress",
				logger.String("path", call.Path), logger.Int("status", call.Status))
		})

	resp, err := c.Get(ctx, "/v1/subscribers", url.Values{"profileId": {"P-tenant-a"}})

Patterns are supplied UNANCHORED and anchored by the constructor. Leaving
anchoring to the caller is exactly the omission that turns an allowlist into a
sieve, and it is invisible in review.

# What the response gives you

Get and Do return a fully-read [Response] rather than an *http.Response. A
returned *http.Response makes the caller responsible for closing the body and
bounding its size, and one forgotten Close leaks a connection. It also makes
an honest byte count impossible, since the size of a body is only known once
it has been read.

A non-2xx status returns BOTH the response and an error: a caller diagnosing
the failure needs the body, and a caller who never considered the status still
gets an error. A 204 with no body is a normal outcome, not a failure.

# What it deliberately does not do

It does not decode. Depending on the codec registry would link every codec
the SDK ships into every consumer that only wanted a guarded GET, so
decoding belongs above this layer.

It does not truncate an oversized body — it fails with [ResponseTooLarge]. A
silent truncation does not stay silent; it resurfaces several layers away as
an incomprehensible decode error on a body that looks complete.

packages.name: http1
packages.doc:
Package http1 is the restricted HTTP/1.1 profile the SDK serves on its loop
engine (ADR 0186 §D6): a codec that frames requests out of bytes and appends
responses to bytes, and HandleLoop, the adapter that serves a Handler on a
loop group of package server.

It is a profile, not an HTTP server, and what it refuses defines it. A
request is answered with its status and Connection: close, and its
connection closed, before any handler sees it, when it carries any
Transfer-Encoding (chunked, and so trailers, included), Expect, a bare CR or
LF, a NUL or another control byte in a value, obs-fold, whitespace before a
colon, a name outside tchar, a Content-Length that is not one run of at most
ten digits or that repeats, a second Authorization or Host, CONNECT, a
target two readers could resolve apart — a dot-segment, an empty segment, a
backslash, an encoded slash, dot, backslash or NUL, an absolute-form not for
its Host — or a head, target or body past its Limits. HTTP/2, Upgrade and
TLS are out of the profile: a program that needs them mounts net/http with Group.HandleHTTP.
Framing depends on neither the method nor the route: a request takes its
head plus its Content-Length.

# Serving

	type api struct{ lanes []perLane } // one per lane, indexed by Request.Lane

	func (a *api) ServeHTTP1(req *http1.Request, res *http1.Response) {
		l := &a.lanes[req.Lane]
		switch req.Route { // set by the router link
		case routeItem:
			res.Defer = true // answered at the end of the batch
			l.pending = append(l.pending, job{res: res, user: req.Auth})
		default:
			res.Status = 404
		}
	}

	func (a *api) EndBatch(lane int) {
		l := &a.lanes[lane]
		// one transaction for every job of l.pending, then for each:
		// job.res.Status, job.res.Body = ..., ...; job.res.Defer = false
	}

	routes, _ := http1.Routes(http1.Route{ID: routeItem, Method: "GET", Path: "/items/", Prefix: true},
		http1.Route{ID: routeHealth, Path: "/health"})
	bearer, _ := http1.Bearer(verifier, routeHealth) // /health needs no token
	srv.Group("api", server.Listen("tcp", ":8080"), server.Loop(server.LoopValue{Loops: 2})).
		HandleLoop(http1.HandleLoop(http1.Chain(a, routes, bearer), http1.Parser{}))

A handler runs on its lane's thread and must not block it. Every callback
of one lane runs on that thread, one at a time, so state kept per lane needs
no lock; Request.Lane and the lane argument of EndBatch name the lane. The
answers of a batch leave at its end, in request order on each connection.

# The chain

A link is a Middleware, composed with Chain, the first listed outermost.
The codec has already computed the request's canonical Path — no
dot-segment, no empty segment, no encoded slash, dot, backslash or NUL, an
absolute-form target reduced to its path once its authority matched Host —
so every link routes and judges the same bytes. Routes sets
Request.Route, Bearer verifies the token for every route its exemptions do
not name and copies the subject and the claims into Request.Auth by value,
Headers gives every answer its fields, and Log hands an AccessLogger a
record of the fields it allows, never a credential. No link writes the
bytes a request takes: the adapter frames with what Parse returned.

# The codec alone

Parser.Parse, AppendResponse and AppendRefusal frame and write without the
loop, on any []byte: nothing allocates once the caller's buffers have room.

packages.name: server
packages.doc:
Package server — the two group options only an HTTP group reads: the header
phase's own deadline and the header size cap.

Package server is the inbound half of the SDK's network domain (ADR 0029):
one unified listener engine for TCP, Unix, TLS and mutual TLS, serving
pluggable handlers grouped behind shared middlewares.

# The whole thing

	srv := server.New()
	srv.Group("echo", server.Listen("tcp", ":8080")).
		HandleFunc(func(ctx context.Context, c server.Conn) error {
			_, err := io.Copy(c, c)
			return err
		})
	err := srv.Serve(ctx)

That is the design target, not a simplified excerpt. [Conn] embeds net.Conn,
so a handler reads and writes a connection exactly as it would any socket and
every io helper keeps working — io.Copy, bufio, encoding wrappers. Everything
the domain adds is additive.

# Groups

A group is a set of listeners sharing one handler, one middleware chain and
one policy. It exists so the same handler can answer on a TCP port and a Unix
socket without wiring it twice:

	srv.Group("api",
		server.Listen("tcp", ":8443"),
		server.Listen("unix", "/run/api.sock"),
		server.TLS(identity),
		server.IdleTimeout(30*time.Second),
	).Use(mw).Handle(handler)

[Group] returns the group rather than a (group, error) pair on purpose: a
declaration mistake — a duplicate name, an unusable address, a missing
handler — is recorded and reported by [Server].Start. The declaration chain
stays readable, and nothing is swallowed.

# TLS and mutual TLS

One option covers both. A [github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/tlsid.Identity]
built with RequireClientCert turns the group's listeners into mutual-TLS
listeners; the same identity type serves the outbound client, so the two
cannot drift apart. The handshake runs on the connection's own goroutine, so
a slow or hostile peer cannot stall the accept path for everyone else.

# Lifecycle

[Server].Start returns once every listener is bound, so a nil error means the
ports are open. [Server].Serve starts, blocks until the context is cancelled,
then drains. [Server].Shutdown stops accepting and waits for in-flight work
within a budget, severing what remains when the budget expires — a shutdown
that never returns is worse than one that admits it gave up.

[Server].State reports the phase, the addresses actually bound, and whether
any listener fell back from a requested optimisation. A silent degradation is
indistinguishable from a working server, so it is surfaced rather than logged
once at startup.

An Accept that fails for any reason but its listener closing — the process
out of file descriptors, typically — is retried after a wait, never at once:
5 ms, doubling, held at one second, started over by the next accepted
connection, as net/http's own Serve does. Retrying at once would spin a core
per listener for as long as the condition lasts. A shutdown during a wait
ends it at once, and [State].AcceptBackoffs counts the waits, so a server
that cannot accept says so.

# Connections that never end

A drain waits for in-flight work to finish, which assumes it eventually does.
An event stream, a long poll, or anything built on a protocol upgrade breaks
that assumption: the request is in flight forever by design, so the drain
waits out its whole budget and then severs the socket under the handler.

[DrainSignal] is the way out. A handler holding a connection open selects on
it alongside its own work and returns when it closes, which turns a
budget-length DRAIN_TIMEOUT into a clean drain:

	select {
	case <-server.DrainSignal(r.Context()):
		return
	case ev := <-events:
		// …
	}

The request context is deliberately NOT cancelled to say this. Cancelling it
would tell every handler to abandon the response it is halfway through, which
is the opposite of what a graceful drain is for. The signal is additive: a
handler that ignores it behaves exactly as it did before.

[github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/sse] is the Server-Sent Events
implementation built on it, and watches the signal for you.

# Protocol upgrades

[github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/websocket] is WebSocket (RFC 6455),
server side. It hijacks the response, which means the socket stops being the
engine's: it is neither closed nor waited for by a drain — the same carve-out
http.Server.Shutdown documents for hijacked connections. The connection
watches [DrainSignal] and closes itself with a 1001 "going away" instead, so
a deployment ends it deliberately rather than by severing it.

The same is true of anything else a handler hijacks: once the socket is taken
over it is the handler's to close.

packages.name: sse
packages.doc:
Package sse is the server side of Server-Sent Events: a unidirectional
server→client stream over an ordinary HTTP response.

# The whole thing

	func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		stream, err := sse.New(w, r)
		if err != nil {
			http.Error(w, "streaming unavailable", http.StatusInternalServerError)
			return
		}
		defer stream.Close()

		for {
			select {
			case <-stream.Done():
				return
			case ev := <-events:
				if err := stream.Send(sse.Event{ID: ev.Cursor, Name: "tick", Data: ev.JSON}); err != nil {
					return
				}
			}
		}
	}

It is written against net/http's own interfaces, so it works in any
http.Handler. Mounted on this SDK's engine — Group.HandleHTTP — it
additionally observes the server's drain signal, which is what stops an
endless stream from holding a graceful shutdown open for its whole budget.

# Why a newline is not an error

The format has no escape mechanism. A line terminator inside a value is not
quoted, it SPLITS the value across several "data:" lines, which the client
rejoins with "\n" — so a multi-line payload is expressible and exact. The
same absence of escaping makes a terminator inside [Event].ID or
[Event].Name unrepresentable, and those are refused rather than truncated: a
silently shortened id is a resume token pointing at the wrong place.

# Reconnection, and what the SDK does not do

A client stores the last non-empty id it saw and sends it back in the
Last-Event-ID header when it reconnects. [Stream].LastEventID hands that
cursor to the handler. Nothing is replayed from it, on purpose.

A replay buffer held by the stream would be empty at exactly the moment a
resume needs it — a reconnect is a NEW connection and therefore a new stream.
A buffer that outlived the stream would be an application store: it has to
know how many events to keep, how long they stay valid, and whether replaying
them is even safe, which are questions about what the events MEAN and not
about the transport. So the cursor is handed over and the handler resumes
from its own log. Minting ids is the handler's job for the same reason: an id
the SDK invented would be a number that means nothing to the application the
client sends it back to.

# Keep-alive

An idle stream is indistinguishable from a dead one to a proxy counting idle
seconds. [Stream] therefore sends a periodic comment — ignored by every
client, so it can never be mistaken for an event. The interval defaults to
[DefaultKeepAlive]; a zero passed to [KeepAlive] is clamped to it rather than
silently meaning "never", and "never" is spelled [WithoutKeepAlive].

# Shutdown

[Stream].Done closes when the client disconnects, when the handler calls
[Stream].Close, or when the server begins draining. [Stream].Send refuses
once it has, so a handler that only ever calls Send in a loop terminates too.
Both halves matter: without the second, one handler shape could still hold a
graceful shutdown open until its budget expired.

# Clients

This package is the server half only. The SDK's outbound client returns a
fully-read body by design and cannot consume a stream that never ends; see
the package CLAUDE.md for why that is a separate decision rather than an
omission.

packages.name: static
packages.doc:
Package static serves a tree of files — a single-page application, a
documentation site, an embed.FS — over HTTP: what http.FileServerFS does,
and what it does not (ADR 0130).

# The whole thing

	//go:embed dist
	var dist embed.FS

	tree, _ := fs.Sub(dist, "dist")
	assets, err := static.New(tree, static.Config{
		SinglePageApp: true,
		Immutable:     func(name string) bool { return strings.HasPrefix(name, "assets/") },
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	mux.Handle("GET /app/", http.StripPrefix("/app", assets))

# What it refuses

  - A request path is cleaned from the root before anything is looked up,
    so no spelling of ".." climbs above the tree — whatever the file
    system itself does with a name.
  - A directory is never listed. It is served by its index.html, after a
    redirect to its name with a trailing slash so the page's relative links
    resolve inside it; a directory with no index.html is a 404.
  - Only GET and HEAD are answered; anything else is a 405 with Allow. HEAD
    answers exactly what GET would, without the body.

# A single-page application

With [Config].SinglePageApp, a path that has no extension and names nothing
is served the root's index.html with a 200, so a client-side route
survives a reload. A path WITH an extension that names nothing stays a 404:
a script tag must never receive a page of HTML in place of the script it
asked for.

# Headers

Every response — a file, a redirect, a 404, a 405, a 500 — carries a
Content-Security-Policy ([DefaultContentSecurityPolicy] unless
[Config].ContentSecurityPolicy names one), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff,
and a Referrer-Policy ([DefaultReferrerPolicy], "same-origin", unless
[Config].ReferrerPolicy names one). [New] refuses a policy holding a control
character, and a Referrer-Policy that is not a list of the tokens the
specification defines, since a browser ignores one it does not know.

Under nosniff a browser refuses a script or a stylesheet served with the
wrong type, and the standard library lets a host's MIME tables override its
own. The types a page cannot run without — HTML, JavaScript, CSS, JSON,
WebAssembly, SVG, a web manifest — are therefore pinned, the same on every
host.

A file [Config].Immutable marks content-hashed is sent with
[ImmutableCacheControl]: cached for a year and never revalidated. Every
other response is sent with [RevalidateCacheControl], so a redeployed page
is never served stale.

# Errors a wrapper can see

Every status goes through the ResponseWriter the handler was given, so a
handler wrapped by one that records the status sees every 5xx. A name the
file system refuses — nothing there, a character it cannot hold, a file
used as a directory, a component too long — is the client's 404, because a
client chooses every name it asks for and could otherwise produce a 5xx at
will. A name the tree holds and cannot open, stat or seek — a permission
refused, a storage failure — is a 500. A failure after the status is sent
cannot change it; the body is cut short of its declared length instead.

packages.name: tlsid
packages.doc:
Package tlsid builds TLS and mutual-TLS identities for the SDK's network
domain (ADR 0029), from files on disk or from material already in memory.

An Identity is opaque and redacts itself: its String and GoString output is
always "<redacted>", so an accidental %v, %s or %#v cannot spill key material
into a log line. The only way out is [Identity].ClientConfig or
[Identity].ServerConfig, each of which mints a fresh *tls.Config, so one
caller's mutation can never reach another.

The package exists to close a specific, widely-repeated bug. The standard
library's x509.CertPool.AppendCertsFromPEM reports failure through a boolean
return that is almost universally discarded, so a CA bundle that is empty,
truncated, or accidentally a private key produces a pool that parses without
complaint and verifies nothing. Here such a bundle is a typed
TLS_MATERIAL_INVALID error. An absent bundle (use the platform trust store)
stays deliberately distinct from an unusable one.

The same principle governs the rest of the surface: a certificate supplied
without its key is refused rather than degraded to an anonymous connection, a
server that demands a client certificate without a CA bundle to verify it
against is refused at construction rather than rejecting every peer at
handshake time, and the minimum version defaults to TLS 1.3 with TLS 1.0 and
1.1 refused outright per RFC 8996. A silent downgrade is always the wrong
answer for transport security, so this package never performs one.

# Loading from disk

	id, err := tlsid.Load(tlsid.FileParams{
		CertFile:   "/etc/pki/client.crt",
		KeyFile:    "/etc/pki/client.key",
		RootsFile:  "/etc/pki/ca.crt",
		ServerName: "sdm.core.svc",
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	conn, err := tls.Dial("tcp", "127.0.0.1:8000", id.ClientConfig())

ServerName is optional in the type and close to mandatory in practice: any
deployment reached through a port forward or a tunnel dials 127.0.0.1 while
the peer certificate names the real service, and the handshake fails until
ServerName overrides the verified name.

# Loading from memory

New takes the same material as bytes, so certificates can come from a secret
manager without ever touching a filesystem:

	id, err := tlsid.New(tlsid.Params{CertPEM: cert, KeyPEM: key, RootsPEM: ca})

# Mutual TLS

Set RequireClientCert on a server identity and supply the CA bundle that
client certificates must chain to:

	id, err := tlsid.Load(tlsid.FileParams{
		CertFile:          "/etc/pki/server.crt",
		KeyFile:           "/etc/pki/server.key",
		ClientCAFile:      "/etc/pki/client-ca.crt",
		RequireClientCert: true,
	})
	ln := tls.NewListener(raw, id.ServerConfig())

packages.name: websocket
packages.doc:
Package websocket is the server side of RFC 6455: an HTTP request upgraded
into a bidirectional, message-oriented connection over the same socket.

# The whole thing

	func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		conn, err := websocket.Upgrade(w, r)
		if err != nil {
			return // Upgrade has already written the HTTP refusal
		}
		defer conn.Close()

		for {
			msg, rerr := conn.Receive()
			if rerr != nil {
				return
			}
			if serr := conn.Send(msg); serr != nil {
				return
			}
		}
	}

It is written against net/http's own interfaces, so it works in any
http.Handler. Mounted on this SDK's engine — Group.HandleHTTP — it
additionally observes the server's drain signal, which is what stops a
connection that by design never ends from being severed under its handler on
every deployment.

# Messages, not frames

[Conn].Receive returns whole messages. Fragmentation is the sender's private
choice of chunk size, not a semantic boundary, so surfacing it would put an
implementation detail of the peer's writer into every consumer. Control
frames — Ping, Pong, Close — are answered underneath and never surface as
messages: they are transport, not payload.

The returned [Message].Data aliases the connection's reassembly buffer and is
valid until the next [Conn].Receive. Keep it longer and you must copy it.
That is what makes a steady-state read allocate nothing.

# What is refused, and why refusing is the specification

RFC 6455 is unusual in how much of it is stated as MUST-fail rather than
should-tolerate, because a frame stream that keeps going after a
disagreement is two endpoints reading different messages from the same bytes.
This implementation refuses:

  - an unmasked client frame (§5.1) — masking is what stops a hostile script
    from steering a browser into emitting bytes a transparent proxy would
    read as a second, attacker-chosen HTTP request;
  - a set reserved bit or a reserved opcode (§5.2);
  - a fragmented or over-125-byte control frame (§5.5);
  - a length not in its minimal encoding (§5.2);
  - a continuation with no message in progress, or a new data frame
    interrupting one (§5.4);
  - a text message that is not valid UTF-8 (§8.1), judged on the reassembled
    message so a sequence straddling a fragment boundary stays valid;
  - a close code that must never travel — 1004, 1005, 1006, 1015 and the
    unallocated ranges (§7.4.2) — in either direction.

# Bounds

A frame announces its length in a 64-bit field the PEER writes.
[MaxFrameSize] is checked against that announcement before a single byte is
read or allocated, and [MaxMessageSize] against the accumulated total, since
fragmentation lets a peer exceed any per-frame bound a thousand small frames
at a time. Neither has an "unbounded" setting on purpose.

# Extensions

None are negotiated, permessage-deflate included. The server sends no
Sec-WebSocket-Extensions header — which RFC 6455 §4.2.2 defines as the way to
say "no extension is in use" — and the frame reader enforces the same answer
by refusing any reserved bit an extension would have set. Compression is
therefore a refusal the wire can verify, not a promise in a document.

# Origin

The browser's same-origin policy does not apply to WebSocket: any page can
open a connection to this server, and the browser attaches the user's cookies
to the handshake. By default an Origin header, when present, must name the
request's own host and port — and, when this server terminates TLS itself,
the https scheme as well, because an http:// page for the same host is
exactly the downgrade the check exists to notice. A request with no Origin (a
CLI, a service, a Go client) is allowed, because there is no ambient
credential to abuse; the opaque "null" origin is refused.

Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, the request reaches this server in
plaintext whatever the browser used, so the default rule cannot see the
scheme. It does not guess it either: a request carrying Forwarded or
X-Forwarded-Proto on a connection this server did not terminate is refused,
with a message naming what to configure. Only the PRESENCE of those headers
is read, never their value — one a client writes can make the check stricter
and never looser. [AllowOrigins] names the origins outright and replaces the
default rule entirely; [AllowAnyOrigin] removes the check, by name.

# One goroutine always reads

Every connection needs exactly one goroutine looping on [Conn].Receive for
its whole life — including a connection the handler only ever writes to.
That loop is where the peer's Ping is answered (RFC 6455 §5.5.2), where its
Close is replied to (§5.5.1), and the only place the heartbeat can see that
the peer is alive. A handler that pushes runs it in a goroutine of its own
and discards what it reads:

	func push(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		conn, err := websocket.Upgrade(w, r)
		if err != nil {
			return
		}
		defer conn.Close()

		go func() { // the reader: required even with nothing to read
			for {
				if _, rerr := conn.Receive(); rerr != nil {
					return
				}
			}
		}()

		for {
			select {
			case <-conn.Done():
				return
			case event := <-events: // the application's own feed
				if serr := conn.SendText(event); serr != nil {
					return
				}
			}
		}
	}

The reading goroutine needs no joining: the deferred Close ends the
connection, and its Receive returns the terminal error.

# Liveness and shutdown

A peer that vanishes without closing leaves a socket that is perfectly
readable and will simply never produce another byte. The heartbeat is the
only thing that turns that silence into an ending: every [PingInterval] it
sends a Ping, and one interval later it ends the connection if the handler
has READ no frame since. It counts frames the handler has read, not frames
that arrived — a Pong the peer sent on time is silence to it until
[Conn].Receive reads it — so a connection nobody reads is ended within two
intervals, about a minute at [DefaultPingInterval], however healthy the peer
is. Zero is clamped to [DefaultPingInterval] rather than meaning "never", and
"never" is spelled [WithoutPing].

[Conn].Done closes when the peer sends Close, when the socket dies, when the
heartbeat gives up, when the handler closes it, or when the server begins
draining — in which case the connection sends a 1001 "going away" of its own
accord. [Conn].Receive and [Conn].Send refuse from the same instant, so the
reading loop and a pushing loop both terminate too.

# Clients

This package is the server half only. The SDK's outbound client returns a
fully-read body by design and cannot dial an upgrade; see the package
CLAUDE.md for why that is a separate decision rather than an omission.

symbols.name: AllowMethods
symbols.doc: AllowMethods admits only the named HTTP methods. Passing none admits none.

symbols.name: AllowPaths
symbols.doc:
AllowPaths admits only paths matching one of the patterns. The patterns are
supplied unanchored and anchored here, so no caller can forget to.

symbols.name: CallFailed

code.public: The outbound call failed

symbols.doc: CallFailed reports an unreachable upstream or a non-2xx status.

symbols.name: CallHook
symbols.doc: CallHook receives one CallInfo per outbound call. It must not block.

symbols.name: CallInfo
symbols.doc: CallInfo records one completed outbound call.

symbols.name: Client
symbols.doc: Client performs guarded outbound HTTP calls.

symbols.name: Config
symbols.doc:
Config describes an outbound client. Durations accept "5s" as well as a raw
nanosecond count, so a configuration file stays readable.

symbols.name: DenyPaths
symbols.doc:
DenyPaths refuses paths matching one of the patterns. A deny is final and is
not overridable by an allow pattern.

symbols.name: Duration
symbols.doc: Duration is a configuration-friendly time.Duration.

symbols.name: New
symbols.spelled: func(cfg Config, id tlsid.Identity, policy Policy, hook CallHook) (c *Client, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(cfg github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/client.Config, id github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/tlsid.Identity, policy github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/client.Policy, hook github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/client.CallHook) (c *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/client.Client, err error)
symbols.doc:
New builds a guarded client. A nil policy is refused rather than defaulted to
"allow everything": an unguarded egress path wearing the name of a guarded one
is worse than no client at all.

symbols.name: Policies
symbols.doc:
Policies requires every policy to allow the request. Composition is by
conjunction, so adding a policy can only ever narrow what is permitted.

symbols.name: Policy
symbols.doc:
Policy authorises an outbound request. Implementations run inside the
transport, so no call site can bypass them.

symbols.name: PolicyFunc
symbols.doc: PolicyFunc adapts a plain function to Policy.

symbols.name: RequestDenied

code.public: The request was refused by policy

symbols.doc:
RequestDenied reports a request refused by the policy. Its public message
never names the refused path, so a denial cannot leak the private API
surface into a log line.

symbols.name: RequestInfo
symbols.doc:
RequestInfo is the immutable request description a Policy judges. It carries
the ESCAPED path: url.URL.Path is already percent-decoded, so a policy that
judged it would accept "%2e%2e", which the upstream reinterprets as "..".

symbols.name: Response
symbols.doc: Response is a fully-read outbound response.

symbols.name: ResponseTooLarge

code.public: The response is larger than the accepted size

symbols.doc: ResponseTooLarge reports a body beyond the configured ceiling.

symbols.name: TooManyRedirects

code.public: The outbound call exceeded its redirect budget

symbols.doc: TooManyRedirects reports a redirect chain beyond the configured cap.

symbols.name: UnsafePath

code.public: The request path is not in normalised form

symbols.doc:
UnsafePath reports a path carrying a dot segment, literal or
percent-encoded, or a path that is not absolute.

symbols.name: Access
symbols.doc:
Access is one request's access-log record, as Log's link hands it to an
AccessLogger.

symbols.name: AccessLogger
symbols.doc: AccessLogger receives Log's records, on the lane's thread.

symbols.name: AppendField
symbols.spelled: func(dst []byte, name string, value string) ([]byte, error)
symbols.canonical: func(dst []byte, name string, value string) ([]byte, error)
symbols.doc:
AppendField appends "name: value\r\n" to dst. A name that is not a token, a
control byte in the value, and Content-Length, Connection and
Transfer-Encoding, which the codec writes, are refused with ResponseInvalid.

symbols.name: AppendRefusal
symbols.doc:
AppendRefusal appends the whole answer to r — its status, Content-Length: 0
and Connection: close; the caller then closes the connection.

symbols.name: AppendResponse
symbols.spelled: func(dst []byte, req *Request, res *Response, closing bool) ([]byte, error)
symbols.canonical: func(dst []byte, req *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/http1.Request, res *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/http1.Response, closing bool) ([]byte, error)
symbols.doc:
AppendResponse appends the whole answer res gives req: the status line,
res.Header, Content-Length from len(res.Body), Connection: close when res,
req or closing asks for it, then the body.

symbols.name: AppendStatusLine
symbols.doc:
AppendStatusLine appends the status line of status to dst; below 200 is
refused with ResponseInvalid.

symbols.name: Auth
symbols.doc:
Auth is what an authenticating link established: a subject and claims,
held by value in the Request.

symbols.name: Batcher
symbols.doc:
Batcher is the optional capability of a Handler served on a loop group:
EndBatch runs once per batch of the loop's requests, before any answer of
the batch is written, and completes the responses the handler deferred.

symbols.name: Bearer
symbols.doc:
Bearer returns the authenticating link: a request whose Route is not in
exempt is answered 401 unless v verifies its Bearer token; v sets the
subject and the claims on the request's Auth, a value.

symbols.name: BearerLayer
symbols.doc: BearerLayer is the link Bearer builds.

symbols.name: BearerVerifier
symbols.doc:
BearerVerifier verifies a Bearer token for Bearer's link and fills the
request's Auth.

symbols.name: BodyTooLarge

code.public: The request content is too large

symbols.doc: BodyTooLarge is the refusal of a Content-Length past the body bound.

symbols.name: Chain
symbols.doc:
Chain applies links to a handler, outermost first: Chain(h, a, b) yields
a(b(h)), the first link listed the first to see a request.

symbols.name: ContentLengthInvalid

code.public: The Content-Length is not valid

symbols.doc:
ContentLengthInvalid is the refusal of a Content-Length that is not one run
of digits, is too long, or repeats.

symbols.name: Continue
symbols.doc:
Continue returns req.Consumed and sets req.Body once buf holds the whole
body of a request whose head Parse framed; until then it returns 0.

symbols.name: DefaultBody
symbols.doc: DefaultBody is the Content-Length bound a zero Limits.Body selects.

symbols.name: DefaultHead
symbols.doc: DefaultHead is the head bound a zero Limits.Head selects, in bytes.

symbols.name: DefaultTarget
symbols.doc: DefaultTarget is the request-target bound a zero Limits.Target selects.

symbols.name: ExpectRefused

code.public: The expectation cannot be met

symbols.doc: ExpectRefused is the refusal of a request carrying Expect.

symbols.name: Field
symbols.doc: Field is one field line of a Request, as it arrived.

symbols.name: FieldDuplicated

code.public: A request field is repeated

symbols.doc: FieldDuplicated is the refusal of a second Authorization or Host field.

symbols.name: HandleLoop
symbols.doc:
HandleLoop adapts h to the loop engine: the handler of
server.Group.HandleLoop. p frames every request; the zero Parser is the
profile's defaults. A refused request is answered and closed without
reaching h; the batch's answers leave at its end, after h's EndBatch when h
is a Batcher, in request order on each connection. A Response starts every
request with a nil Header and Body, which h points at bytes it owns until
the answer is taken. An answer the writer refuses, or one left deferred, is
answered 500 and its connection closed; one the connection's output refuses
closes the connection.

symbols.name: Handler
symbols.doc:
Handler answers one request of the profile. It sees only requests the
codec framed and accepted, fills the Response, and the codec writes the
framing: the status line, Content-Length and Connection: close.

symbols.name: HandlerFunc
symbols.doc: HandlerFunc adapts a plain function to Handler.

symbols.name: HeadTooLarge

code.public: The request header is too large

symbols.doc: HeadTooLarge is the refusal of a head past its bound, or of too many fields.

symbols.name: Headers
symbols.doc:
Headers returns the link that gives every answer the field lines pairs
names, name then value; a name AppendField refuses is Misconfigured.

symbols.name: HeadersLayer
symbols.doc: HeadersLayer is the link Headers builds.

symbols.name: Limits
symbols.doc:
Limits bounds what one request may carry. Zero selects the profile's
default, never unbounded.

symbols.name: Log
symbols.doc:
Log returns the access-log link: one Access record per request, with the
request fields allow names. Authorization, Proxy-Authorization and Cookie
are refused with Misconfigured: a credential is never logged.

symbols.name: LogLayer
symbols.doc: LogLayer is the link Log builds.

symbols.name: LoopHandler
symbols.doc:
LoopHandler serves the profile on a loop group: the server.LoopHandler
HandleLoop returns.

symbols.name: MaxAccessFields
symbols.doc: MaxAccessFields is how many request fields Log may allow.

symbols.name: MaxBody
symbols.doc: MaxBody is the largest Content-Length bound Limits.Body may ask for.

symbols.name: MaxFields
symbols.doc:
MaxFields is how many field lines one request may carry; one more is
refused (431).

symbols.name: MaxHead
symbols.doc: MaxHead is the largest head bound Limits.Head may ask for.

symbols.name: MaxSubject
symbols.doc: MaxSubject is the longest subject an Auth holds, in bytes.

symbols.name: MethodUnsupported

code.public: The request method is not supported

symbols.doc: MethodUnsupported is the refusal of CONNECT.

symbols.name: Middleware
symbols.doc:
Middleware is a link of a chain: it decorates a Handler with another,
composed by Chain.

symbols.name: Misconfigured

code.public: The HTTP/1.1 profile limits are not valid

symbols.doc: Misconfigured is a Limits NewParser refuses.

symbols.name: NewParser
symbols.doc:
NewParser returns a Parser bounded by l, refusing a negative or oversized
bound with Misconfigured.

symbols.name: Parser
symbols.doc:
Parser frames requests under its Limits. The zero Parser uses the
profile's defaults; NewParser validates others.

symbols.name: Pending
symbols.doc:
Pending returns how many bytes of req's body have yet to arrive when
buffered bytes of the request are held.

symbols.name: Refusal
symbols.doc:
Refusal names the rule a request broke; RefusalNone is none. Branch on its
Err, a sentinel of this package, and log its String.

symbols.name: RefusalNone
symbols.doc: RefusalNone is no refusal: the request was framed, or needs more bytes.

symbols.name: Request
symbols.doc:
Request is one request, framed by the codec. Every slice aliases the bytes
Request is one request, framed by the codec. Every slice aliases the bytes
it was framed from; Lane names the lane that framed it, Path is its
canonical path, Route and Auth what the chain's links set.

symbols.name: RequestMalformed

code.public: The request is malformed

symbols.doc:
RequestMalformed is the refusal of a request whose syntax the profile does
not accept: its request line, a name, a bare CR or LF, a control byte.

symbols.name: Response
symbols.doc:
Response is the answer a Handler gives: a status, extra field lines written
by AppendField, a body, Close, and Defer to answer at the batch's end.

symbols.name: ResponseInvalid

code.public: The response is not valid

symbols.doc: ResponseInvalid is a response the writer refuses to write.

symbols.name: Route
symbols.doc:
Route is one route of Routes' link: an identifier, a method, a canonical
path and whether it is a prefix.

symbols.name: RouteLayer
symbols.doc: RouteLayer is the link Routes builds.

symbols.name: Routes
symbols.doc:
Routes returns the router link: Request.Route is the first route whose
Method and Path match, zero for none, and the next handler runs either
way. A bad ID, a repeated one, a Path not from "/" or a Method that is not
a token is refused with Misconfigured.

symbols.name: TargetTooLong

code.public: The request target is too long

symbols.doc: TargetTooLong is the refusal of a request-target past its bound.

symbols.name: TransferEncoding

code.public: Transfer-Encoding is not supported

symbols.doc: TransferEncoding is the refusal of any Transfer-Encoding, chunked included.

symbols.name: Worker
symbols.doc:
Worker is the optional capability of a Handler served on a loop group that
answers off the loop's thread: a Response marked Pending is filled by
WorkHTTP1 on the lane's worker goroutine, which may block, and written once
it returns.

symbols.name: Adopt
symbols.doc:
Adopt takes over a socket inherited from a supervisor instead of binding one.

Socket activation is what makes a zero-downtime restart possible: the
supervisor holds the bound socket across the exec, so no connection is lost
and no bind races. The name is the one the unit file publishes in
LISTEN_FDNAMES. Repeat the option to adopt several sockets into one group.

A named socket the supervisor did not pass is SocketAdoptFailed, never a
silent fallback to binding: a service that quietly binds its own port has
lost exactly the property activation exists to provide. The same holds on
Windows, which has no socket activation at all: Start fails there with
SocketAdoptFailed, whose cause field names UNSUPPORTED_PLATFORM.

symbols.name: AlreadyStarted

code.public: The server is already started

symbols.doc: AlreadyStarted reports a second Start on a running server.

symbols.name: BatchReplies
symbols.doc:
BatchReplies makes a datagram group's replies leave per read batch: Reply
then reports a queued reply sent, and a queued send that fails — when the batch
ends, or earlier when the queue fills — is counted in
[State].Datagrams.ReplyFailures; a reply too large to queue is written at once
and returns its own error. On Linux a UDP socket batches
them with sendmmsg and, where it can, UDP GSO; elsewhere each leaves with a
WriteTo. Under it Reply is valid only during the handler's call, as Data is.
Without it, Reply writes at once and returns the write's own error. A stream
group refuses it.

symbols.name: BatchSize
symbols.doc:
BatchSize sets how many datagrams one read attempts to collect. One disables
batching; zero selects the platform default. Where the platform cannot batch,
State reports the degradation rather than hiding it.

symbols.name: Capability
symbols.doc:
Capability names one engine of the lattice iouring > epoll > portable >
goroutine; its values are the operator's tokens.

symbols.name: CapabilityEpoll
symbols.doc: CapabilityEpoll is epoll, below io_uring.

symbols.name: CapabilityGoroutine
symbols.doc: CapabilityGoroutine is the goroutine engine, the bottom of the lattice.

symbols.name: CapabilityIOURing
symbols.doc: CapabilityIOURing is io_uring, the top of the lattice.

symbols.name: CapabilityPortable
symbols.doc: CapabilityPortable is the portable loop backend, the loop family's floor.

symbols.name: CapabilityURingDeferTaskrun
symbols.doc: CapabilityURingDeferTaskrun opts a loop group into uring-defer-taskrun, a class A-code kernel capability.

symbols.name: CapabilityURingNoSQArray
symbols.doc: CapabilityURingNoSQArray opts a loop group into uring-no-sqarray, a class A-code kernel capability.

symbols.name: CapabilityURingRingFDs
symbols.doc: CapabilityURingRingFDs opts a loop group into uring-ring-fds, a class A-code kernel capability.

symbols.name: CapabilityURingSQRewind
symbols.doc: CapabilityURingSQRewind opts a loop group into uring-sq-rewind, a class A-code kernel capability.

symbols.name: CapabilityValue
symbols.doc: CapabilityValue reports one optional kernel capability of a loop group.

symbols.name: Chain
symbols.doc:
Chain applies middlewares to a handler, outermost first.

Chain(h, a, b, c) yields a(b(c(h))): the first middleware listed is the first
to see a connection, matching how the list reads at the call site.

symbols.name: ChainPacket
symbols.doc: ChainPacket applies middlewares to a datagram handler, outermost first.

symbols.name: Conn
symbols.doc: Conn is one accepted stream connection. It embeds net.Conn.

symbols.name: ConnLimitReached

code.public: The server is at its connection limit

symbols.doc: ConnLimitReached reports a connection turned away by the group ceiling.

symbols.name: DatagramState
symbols.doc:
DatagramState counts what the batched datagram paths drop: messages cut
short, GSO sends refused for their size, queued replies that did not leave.

symbols.name: DrainSignal
symbols.doc:
DrainSignal returns the channel closed when the server serving this request
begins draining, or nil when none is published.

It is how a handler that holds a connection open indefinitely — an event
stream, a long poll — learns that finishing now is the cooperative thing to
do. Without it such a handler holds the drain open until the budget expires
and its socket is severed under it, on every shutdown.

A nil channel blocks forever, so a select that watches it needs no nil check
and behaves correctly on a server that publishes nothing.

symbols.name: DrainTimeout

code.public: The server did not drain before its deadline

symbols.doc: DrainTimeout reports a shutdown whose budget expired with work in flight.

symbols.name: Engine
symbols.doc:
Engine names the engine family the group runs on: EngineGoroutine, one
goroutine per connection, or EngineLoop, the loop engine; Loop then picks the
loop's backend. The zero value, EngineAuto, lets the handler's type choose.
An engine the group's handler cannot run on, or that another option
contradicts — EngineGoroutine with Loop or HandleLoop, EngineLoop with
Handle, HandleFunc or HandleHTTP or on a datagram group — fails Start with
EngineUnsupported, and is never replaced by the other engine.

symbols.name: EngineAuto
symbols.doc: EngineAuto lets the group's handler type choose its engine.

symbols.name: EngineGoroutine
symbols.doc: EngineGoroutine is the default engine, one goroutine per connection.

symbols.name: EngineLoop
symbols.doc: EngineLoop is the loop engine; Loop picks its backend.

symbols.name: EngineUnsupported

code.public: The group's engine cannot serve its handler

symbols.doc: EngineUnsupported reports an Engine the group's handler or options cannot run on.

symbols.name: EngineValue
symbols.doc:
EngineValue names the engine family a group runs on, passed by Engine. The
zero value, EngineAuto, lets the handler's type choose.

symbols.name: EnvDisable
symbols.doc: EnvDisable is the variable that switches engines off.

symbols.name: EnvEngine
symbols.doc: EnvEngine is the variable that caps every group's engine.

symbols.name: Fallbacks
symbols.doc: Fallbacks counts the engine fallbacks and keeps the last one.

symbols.name: Fault
symbols.doc: Fault reports one thing the server runs without, or cannot do, now.

symbols.name: Group
symbols.doc:
Group is a set of listeners sharing one handler, middleware chain and policy.

Group.HandleHTTP mounts an http.Handler on the group's listeners: the group
keeps its own limits, TLS identity and drain, and net/http only does the
protocol.

symbols.name: GroupDuplicate

code.public: The listener group is already declared

symbols.doc: GroupDuplicate reports a second group declared under one name.

symbols.name: GroupNameConflict

code.public: The group's name is not consistent

symbols.doc: GroupNameConflict reports a Name that is empty or contradicts the group's declared name.

symbols.name: GroupOption
symbols.doc: GroupOption configures a Group.

symbols.name: Handler
symbols.doc: Handler serves one accepted stream connection.

symbols.name: HandlerAlreadySet

code.public: The listener group already has a handler

symbols.doc: HandlerAlreadySet reports a second handler declared on one stream group.

symbols.name: HandlerFunc
symbols.doc: HandlerFunc adapts a plain function to Handler.

symbols.name: HandlerMissing

code.public: The listener group has no handler

symbols.doc: HandlerMissing reports a group declared without a handler.

symbols.name: HandshakeTimeout
symbols.doc:
HandshakeTimeout bounds the TLS negotiation on the group's listeners.

Unset does not mean unbounded, unlike the other three. The handshake runs on
the connection's own goroutine — the listener does not negotiate in Accept,
which is what keeps one slow peer from stalling the accept path for everyone
— so it is the one phase that can be stalled before any handler exists to
notice, and a peer that connects and says nothing would otherwise hold a
goroutine and a slot under MaxConns indefinitely. It falls back to a domain
default instead.

symbols.name: IdleTimeout
symbols.doc:
IdleTimeout bounds how long a connection may sit with no traffic at all.

It is enforced on the read side, where silence is observable: a read is
bounded by whichever of ReadTimeout and IdleTimeout is tighter. Setting both
therefore narrows the bound rather than replacing it, which is what the two
options together are asking for.

symbols.name: InvalidAddress

code.public: The network address is not valid

symbols.doc: InvalidAddress reports an unusable listen address.

symbols.name: Listen
symbols.doc:
Listen adds an address to a group. Repeat it to bind several addresses to one
handler — a TCP port and a Unix socket, for instance.

On Windows, whose AF_UNIX sockets are stream-only, a "unixgram" or
"unixpacket" address fails Start with the SDK's UNSUPPORTED_PLATFORM, before
any socket is opened; "unix" is served there as everywhere else.

symbols.name: ListenFailed

code.public: The server could not bind its listening address

symbols.doc: ListenFailed reports a listener that could not be bound.

symbols.name: ListenerState
symbols.doc: ListenerState reports one bound listener, including any fallback.

symbols.name: Loop
symbols.doc:
Loop configures a group's loop engine (ADR 0186 §D5): its backend, its loops
and rings, and its per-connection and pressure bounds. It is judged at Start,
once the group's handler is known: a group served by HandleLoop runs on it,
and a group served by Handle, HandleFunc or HandleHTTP refuses it with
LoopOptionUnsupported, whichever order the declarations came in. A group with
no handler fails with HandlerMissing instead, and one given a second handler
with HandlerAlreadySet. A datagram group refuses it with LoopOptionUnsupported
too. A group served by HandleLoop without it runs on the zero LoopValue.

symbols.name: LoopBackend
symbols.doc: LoopBackend names the mechanic a loop group runs on.

symbols.name: LoopBackendAuto
symbols.doc: LoopBackendAuto takes the best backend the platform's probe reaches.

symbols.name: LoopBackendEpoll
symbols.doc: LoopBackendEpoll is epoll, on every Linux architecture.

symbols.name: LoopBackendIOURing
symbols.doc: LoopBackendIOURing is io_uring, after the kernel's staged probe.

symbols.name: LoopBackendPortable
symbols.doc:
LoopBackendPortable is the default engine's accept path, serialised onto
one handler goroutine.

symbols.name: LoopBackendUnavailable

code.public: The requested loop backend is not available on this kernel

symbols.doc: LoopBackendUnavailable reports an explicit loop backend the kernel's probe refused.

symbols.name: LoopCapabilityRefused

code.public: The loop group asks for a capability it cannot opt into

symbols.doc: LoopCapabilityRefused reports a LoopValue.Capabilities entry a loop group cannot opt into.

symbols.name: LoopConnRef
symbols.doc:
LoopConnRef names one connection of a loop by ring, slot and generation. The
zero value names no connection.

symbols.name: LoopGroupStalled

code.public: A loop group stopped accepting connections

symbols.doc: LoopGroupStalled reports a loop group every ring of which its watchdog drained.

symbols.name: LoopHandler
symbols.doc:
LoopHandler serves the connections of a loop group, one callback per event,
on the loop's thread. A callback must not block it.

symbols.name: LoopIO
symbols.doc:
LoopIO is what a loop offers its handler: Write, Close, SetDeadline and
Pressure on its connections, from a callback, and Post from any goroutine.

symbols.name: LoopJobValue
symbols.doc: LoopJobValue is one job a lane sends its worker.

symbols.name: LoopLayer
symbols.doc:
LoopLayer is the base a loop middleware's layer embeds: it forwards the
eight callbacks to the handler it wraps.

symbols.name: LoopLayered
symbols.doc:
LoopLayered is what every layer of a loop middleware implements: Next is
the handler it wraps.

symbols.name: LoopMiddleware
symbols.doc: LoopMiddleware decorates a loop handler with a layer, for UseLoop.

symbols.name: LoopMiddlewareInvalid

code.public: A loop middleware does not forward every callback

symbols.doc: LoopMiddlewareInvalid reports a loop middleware whose layer does not forward every callback.

symbols.name: LoopNoDescriptors

code.public: The process has no file descriptor available for the loop

symbols.doc: LoopNoDescriptors reports a loop group with no RLIMIT_NOFILE to size it by.

symbols.name: LoopOffloader
symbols.doc:
LoopOffloader is the optional capability of a LoopHandler that offloads
blocking work to one worker goroutine per lane (R3).

symbols.name: LoopOptionHonourer
symbols.doc:
LoopOptionHonourer is the optional capability of a LoopHandler that honours
group options the loop engine does not.

symbols.name: LoopOptionUnsupported

code.public: The group option is not supported by its engine

symbols.doc: LoopOptionUnsupported reports a group option a loop group cannot honour.

symbols.name: LoopOutbound
symbols.doc:
LoopOutbound is one lane's preallocated queue to its worker; Send never
blocks.

symbols.name: LoopOutboundFull

code.public: The server cannot take more offloaded work now

symbols.doc: LoopOutboundFull reports a job refused by a lane's full queue to its worker.

symbols.name: LoopOutboundValue
symbols.doc:
LoopOutboundValue is what an offloader is given at Start: the lanes'
outbounds and the output ceiling of one connection.

symbols.name: LoopOutputFull

code.public: The connection cannot take more output now

symbols.doc: LoopOutputFull reports a Write past a connection's or a loop's output bound.

symbols.name: LoopPostQueueFull

code.public: The loop cannot take more posted work now

symbols.doc: LoopPostQueueFull reports a Post refused by a full queue.

symbols.name: LoopRingState
symbols.doc: LoopRingState reports one ring of one loop group.

symbols.name: LoopSpillFull

code.public: The connection sent more than it may hold unread

symbols.doc: LoopSpillFull reports a connection closed for unconsumed input past its ceiling.

symbols.name: LoopStaleRef

code.public: The connection is closed

symbols.doc: LoopStaleRef reports an operation on a connection that has closed.

symbols.name: LoopStarter
symbols.doc:
LoopStarter is the optional capability of a LoopHandler that keeps state
per lane: OnStart gives it the lane count, once, before any other callback.

symbols.name: LoopState
symbols.doc:
LoopState reports one loop group: its backend, how it got there, how it is
sized, and its rings' counters.

symbols.name: LoopTLSUnsupported

code.public: The loop engine does not serve TLS

symbols.doc: LoopTLSUnsupported reports TLS set on a loop group.

symbols.name: LoopValue
symbols.doc:
LoopValue configures a group's loop engine, passed by Loop. Every field is
optional: zero selects the domain default.

symbols.name: LoopWorker
symbols.doc: LoopWorker runs a lane's offloaded jobs, off the loop's thread; it may block.

symbols.name: LoopWrongThread

code.public: The operation was called outside its loop

symbols.doc: LoopWrongThread reports, under loopdebug, a loop operation off the loop's thread.

symbols.name: LoopsAuto
symbols.doc:
LoopsAuto, as LoopValue.Loops, runs one loop per GOMAXPROCS, read once at
Start.

symbols.name: MaxConns
symbols.doc:
MaxConns caps how many connections a group serves at once.

The budget is per group, not per socket: a group listening on a TCP port and
a Unix socket, or sharded across several listeners, shares one ceiling —
which is what an operator sizing a server actually means. Beyond it a
connection is accepted and closed immediately with ConnLimitReached, because
a refusal the peer can observe beats a timeout it cannot tell from a hang.
Zero means no ceiling.

symbols.name: MaxHeaderBytes
symbols.doc:
MaxHeaderBytes caps the bytes net/http reads for a request's line and header
fields; a request past the cap is answered 431 Request Header Fields Too
Large and never reaches the handler.

Unset (or non-positive) keeps net/http's default of 1 MiB, which applied
silently before this option existed. net/http reads a small fixed allowance
past the cap before refusing. No effect on a group that does not serve HTTP.

symbols.name: MaxPacketSize
symbols.doc:
MaxPacketSize caps the datagram size a group accepts.

A larger datagram is dropped and counted in [State].OversizedPackets, never
delivered. Truncating would hand the handler a prefix indistinguishable from
a complete message, which is a correctness problem rather than a capacity
one; a drop it can observe in State is the honest answer.

symbols.name: Middleware
symbols.doc: Middleware decorates a handler with another of the same type.

symbols.name: Name
symbols.doc:
Name names the group in State, logs and errors. On a group declared with an
empty name it sets the name, which must then be unique like any other; on one
declared with a name it must repeat it. An empty Name, or one that differs
from a non-empty declared name, fails Start with GroupNameConflict.

symbols.name: New
symbols.doc: New builds a server.

symbols.name: NewLoopLayer
symbols.doc:
NewLoopLayer returns the LoopLayer a loop middleware's layer embeds over
next, forwarding every callback to it.

symbols.name: Option
symbols.doc: Option configures a Server.

symbols.name: OptionAdopt
symbols.doc: OptionAdopt is Adopt. The loop engine honours it.

symbols.name: OptionBatchReplies
symbols.doc: OptionBatchReplies is BatchReplies. A datagram group honours it; a stream group refuses it.

symbols.name: OptionBatchSize
symbols.doc: OptionBatchSize is BatchSize.

symbols.name: OptionEngine
symbols.doc: OptionEngine is Engine. Every engine honours it, or refuses the group.

symbols.name: OptionHandshakeTimeout
symbols.doc: OptionHandshakeTimeout is HandshakeTimeout.

symbols.name: OptionIdleTimeout
symbols.doc: OptionIdleTimeout is IdleTimeout. The loop engine honours it.

symbols.name: OptionKind
symbols.doc: OptionKind names a group option, for LoopOptionHonourer.Honours.

symbols.name: OptionLoopMiddleware
symbols.doc: OptionLoopMiddleware is UseLoop. A group no loop handler serves refuses it.

symbols.name: OptionMaxConns
symbols.doc: OptionMaxConns is MaxConns. The loop engine honours it.

symbols.name: OptionMaxHeaderBytes
symbols.doc:
OptionMaxHeaderBytes is MaxHeaderBytes, which only a protocol adapter can
honour.

symbols.name: OptionMaxPacketSize
symbols.doc: OptionMaxPacketSize is MaxPacketSize.

symbols.name: OptionMiddleware
symbols.doc: OptionMiddleware is Use. A loop group always refuses it.

symbols.name: OptionName
symbols.doc: OptionName is Name. Every engine honours it.

symbols.name: OptionNone
symbols.doc: OptionNone names no option; it is the zero value.

symbols.name: OptionPlaintext
symbols.doc: OptionPlaintext is Plaintext. Every engine honours it.

symbols.name: OptionPreHandshake
symbols.doc: OptionPreHandshake is PreHandshake.

symbols.name: OptionReadBufferSize
symbols.doc: OptionReadBufferSize is ReadBufferSize.

symbols.name: OptionReadHeaderTimeout
symbols.doc:
OptionReadHeaderTimeout is ReadHeaderTimeout, which only a protocol adapter
can honour.

symbols.name: OptionReadTimeout
symbols.doc: OptionReadTimeout is ReadTimeout.

symbols.name: OptionShards
symbols.doc: OptionShards is Shards.

symbols.name: OptionTLS
symbols.doc: OptionTLS is TLS. A loop group always refuses it.

symbols.name: OptionWriteTimeout
symbols.doc: OptionWriteTimeout is WriteTimeout.

symbols.name: Override
symbols.doc:
Override reports what KITSUNIUM_NET_ENGINE and KITSUNIUM_NET_DISABLE did to
the engines.

symbols.name: Packet
symbols.doc: Packet is one received datagram.

symbols.name: PacketGroup
symbols.doc: PacketGroup is a set of datagram sockets sharing one handler and chain.

symbols.name: PacketHandler
symbols.doc: PacketHandler serves one received datagram.

symbols.name: PacketHandlerFunc
symbols.doc: PacketHandlerFunc adapts a plain function to PacketHandler.

symbols.name: PacketMiddleware
symbols.doc: PacketMiddleware decorates a datagram handler.

symbols.name: Phase
symbols.doc: Phase is where a server sits in its lifecycle.

symbols.name: PhaseDraining
symbols.doc: PhaseDraining has stopped accepting and is waiting for in-flight work.

symbols.name: PhaseNew
symbols.doc:
The lifecycle phases, in the order a server passes through them. They are
re-exported so a caller can compare State().Phase without importing the
internal package, which Go's firewall forbids anyway.
PhaseNew is a constructed server that has not bound anything yet.

symbols.name: PhaseServing
symbols.doc: PhaseServing is bound and accepting.

symbols.name: PhaseStarting
symbols.doc: PhaseStarting is binding listeners; some may already be up.

symbols.name: PhaseStopped
symbols.doc: PhaseStopped has released every listener.

symbols.name: Plaintext
symbols.doc:
Plaintext declares that the group serves no TLS. Every engine honours it. A
group given both Plaintext and TLS, in either order, fails Start with
PlaintextWithTLS. It is not yet required of a plaintext group: the simple
API will require it of every HTTP group without TLS.

symbols.name: PlaintextWithTLS

code.public: The group cannot be both plaintext and TLS

symbols.doc: PlaintextWithTLS reports a group given both Plaintext and TLS.

symbols.name: Platform
symbols.doc: Platform names the operating system, its release and the toolchain.

symbols.name: PostFunc
symbols.doc:
PostFunc is an operation posted to a loop with LoopIO.Post. It runs once, on
the loop's thread.

symbols.name: ReadBufferSize
symbols.doc:
ReadBufferSize sizes the per-connection scratch buffer handed to the handler
by Conn.Buffer. It is recycled with the connection, which is what lets a
handler read without allocating per connection.

symbols.name: ReadHeaderTimeout
symbols.doc:
ReadHeaderTimeout bounds the HEADER phase of an HTTP request on its own: the
request line and every header field must arrive within d, whatever the read
timeout allows a body.

The header phase is the one a slowloris stalls — a byte every few seconds,
never finishing a line — and the one an honest client finishes in
milliseconds, so it deserves a bound far shorter than a read timeout sized
for an upload. A client that stalls there is disconnected at d. Unset (or
non-positive) keeps the earlier behaviour: the header phase is bounded by
[ReadTimeout]. No effect on a group that does not serve HTTP.

symbols.name: ReadTimeout
symbols.doc:
ReadTimeout bounds one read from the peer.

It is refreshed per read, not installed once when the connection is accepted:
a deadline set at accept time would be a budget for the connection's whole
life, which a peer trickling one byte at a time stays comfortably inside. On
a group serving an http.Handler it bounds three things: each read
of a request body, refreshed before every read — never net/http's own
ReadTimeout, which budgets the whole request and would cut off a peer whose
every read is inside the bound —, the header phase, unless
[ReadHeaderTimeout] sets it apart, and the wait for the next request when
no [IdleTimeout] is set. The time a handler spends between two reads is its
own, and the deadline is cleared once the body has ended.

symbols.name: Server
symbols.doc: Server owns a set of listener groups and their lifecycle.

symbols.name: Shards
symbols.doc:
Shards sets how many listeners to open on each of the group's addresses.

Zero selects one per core; one disables sharding. Where the platform (Windows
has no SO_REUSEPORT) or the socket family (a Unix socket) cannot shard, the
count collapses to one. An explicit count that collapses is reported in State
with the reason; zero collapsing is not, since it asked for nothing a single
listener fails to give.

symbols.name: State
symbols.doc: State is a snapshot of the server's lifecycle and listeners.

symbols.name: TLS
symbols.doc:
TLS turns the group's listeners into TLS listeners, or mutual-TLS ones when
the identity requires a client certificate.

symbols.name: UnsupportedNetwork

code.public: The network type is not supported

symbols.doc: UnsupportedNetwork reports a socket family the domain does not serve.

symbols.name: WithDrainGrace
symbols.doc:
WithDrainGrace sets how long Shutdown keeps accepting and serving once
readiness has turned false, before it closes any listener. Zero closes at
once.

symbols.name: WithDrainTimeout
symbols.doc:
WithDrainTimeout bounds how long Shutdown waits for in-flight connections
before severing them.

symbols.name: WriteTimeout
symbols.doc: WriteTimeout bounds one write to the peer, refreshed per write.

symbols.name: AppendEvent
symbols.doc:
AppendEvent appends ev's wire form to dst and returns the extended slice —
the bytes [Stream].Send writes, for a caller that frames events onto a
transport of its own.

It appends nothing when the frame is invalid: the whole frame is validated
first, so a partial frame never reaches dst. Appending rather than returning
a fresh slice is what lets a caller reuse one buffer for every frame.

symbols.name: ContentType
symbols.doc:
ContentType is the media type an event stream is served under. A client that
receives anything else does not open an EventSource at all.

symbols.name: DefaultKeepAlive
symbols.doc:
DefaultKeepAlive is the comment cadence a stream uses when the caller sets
none. It sits under the idle timeout of every proxy worth naming.

symbols.name: DefaultWriteTimeout
symbols.doc:
DefaultWriteTimeout bounds ONE frame's write. A stream has no total write
budget by nature; this is what stops a peer that has stopped reading from
pinning a goroutine forever.

symbols.name: DrainSignal
symbols.doc:
DrainSignal returns the channel closed when the server serving this request
begins draining, or nil when it publishes none.

It is what [Stream] watches, exposed because an event stream is not the only
handler that holds a connection open indefinitely — a long poll does too, and
so will anything built on a protocol upgrade. A nil channel blocks forever,
so a select that watches it needs no nil check.

symbols.name: Event
symbols.doc:
Event is one Server-Sent Events frame. [Event].Validate reports whether the
wire format can carry it; [AppendEvent] writes it.

symbols.name: FieldInvalid

code.public: The event cannot be represented in the event-stream format

symbols.doc:
FieldInvalid reports an event the wire format cannot carry: a line
terminator in an id, an event name or a comment; a negative or
sub-millisecond retry; an event name with no data, which every client
discards; or a frame with no field at all.

symbols.name: FlushUnsupported

code.public: The response cannot be streamed

symbols.doc:
FlushUnsupported reports a ResponseWriter that cannot be flushed, and so
cannot stream at all.

symbols.name: KeepAlive
symbols.doc:
KeepAlive sets the interval between keep-alive comments.

Zero does not mean "never": a stream with keep-alive silently disabled works
perfectly on a developer's loopback and dies at one minute behind a real
proxy, which is the worst possible place to learn it. Zero is clamped to
[DefaultKeepAlive]; a negative interval is refused. To disable it, say so
with [WithoutKeepAlive].

symbols.name: LastEventIDHeader
symbols.doc:
LastEventIDHeader is the request header a reconnecting client sends, carrying
the id of the last event it processed.

symbols.name: MinRetry
symbols.doc:
MinRetry is the shortest reconnection hint [Event].Retry can carry. The wire
field is an integer millisecond count, so anything shorter would round to
zero — which does not mean "very soon", it means "reconnect immediately".

symbols.name: New
symbols.spelled: func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, opts ...Option) (stream *Stream, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(w net/http.ResponseWriter, r *net/http.Request, opts ...github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/sse.Option) (stream *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/sse.Stream, err error)
symbols.doc:
New starts an event stream on w and returns it.

It writes the response headers and flushes them immediately, so the client
connects at once rather than at the first event. It fails when the response
cannot be flushed — checked before anything is written, so the handler is
free to answer some other way.

symbols.name: Option
symbols.doc: Option configures a Stream.

symbols.name: Retry
symbols.doc:
Retry sets the reconnection delay the stream advertises in its opening frame.

It is the server's one chance to control how hard clients come back: a fleet
that all reconnect on the browser default of about three seconds is a
thundering herd aimed at a server that has just restarted. Zero sends no
retry field.

symbols.name: Stream
symbols.doc:
Stream is one open event stream: an HTTP response held open, written one
frame at a time and flushed after each. It is safe for concurrent use.

symbols.name: StreamClosed

code.public: The event stream is closed

symbols.doc:
StreamClosed reports a send on a stream that has already ended — the
client disconnected, the server began draining, or the handler closed it.
It is the terminal outcome a streaming handler loops until.

symbols.name: StreamMisconfigured

code.public: The event stream options are not valid

symbols.doc:
StreamMisconfigured reports an option the domain refuses to interpret
rather than guess at, such as a negative keep-alive interval.

symbols.name: WithoutKeepAlive
symbols.doc:
WithoutKeepAlive disables the keep-alive comment entirely, so that "never" is
something a caller writes on purpose rather than something a zero does to
them.

symbols.name: WriteTimeout
symbols.doc:
WriteTimeout bounds how long one frame's write may take.

It is per-frame on purpose. A group's WriteTimeout is an absolute deadline
for the whole response, which on an endless stream means the stream is cut at
that instant; a stream replaces it with this bound, refreshed per frame. Zero
is clamped to [DefaultWriteTimeout], negative is refused.

symbols.name: Config
symbols.doc:
Config says how a tree is served; its zero value is a working, strict
configuration.

symbols.name: DefaultContentSecurityPolicy
symbols.doc:
DefaultContentSecurityPolicy is the policy sent when Config names none: the
page's own origin for everything it loads, no base URL or form target
elsewhere, and no framing by another page.

symbols.name: DefaultReferrerPolicy
symbols.doc:
DefaultReferrerPolicy is the Referrer-Policy sent when Config names none: a
full referrer to this origin, none at all to another.

symbols.name: Handler
symbols.doc:
Handler serves one file tree; it is an http.Handler, safe for concurrent
use. The zero Handler has no tree and answers every request 500.

symbols.name: ImmutableCacheControl
symbols.doc:
ImmutableCacheControl is the Cache-Control of a file Config.Immutable marks
content-hashed: a year, shared caches included, never revalidated.

symbols.name: Misconfigured

code.public: The static file handler configuration is not valid

symbols.doc:
Misconfigured is returned by New for a nil tree, a header value holding a
control character, or a Referrer-Policy that is not a list of known tokens.
The "option" field names which; the value is never repeated.

symbols.name: New
symbols.doc:
New returns a Handler serving fsys as cfg says, or Misconfigured. It reads
nothing from fsys. To serve a sub-directory, hand it the result of fs.Sub;
to keep a link inside the tree from leading out of it, hand it an os.Root's
FS rather than os.DirFS — the handler confines the names it is asked for,
not what the tree's own entries point at.

symbols.name: RevalidateCacheControl
symbols.doc:
RevalidateCacheControl is the Cache-Control of every other response:
stored, but revalidated before each use.

symbols.name: FileParams
symbols.doc: FileParams names TLS material to read from the filesystem.

symbols.name: HandshakeFailed

code.public: The TLS handshake failed

symbols.doc: HandshakeFailed reports a TLS or mutual-TLS handshake that did not complete.

symbols.name: Identity
symbols.doc:
Identity is an opaque TLS identity. Its String and GoString output is always
"<redacted>"; ClientConfig and ServerConfig are the only ways to reach the
material, and each returns a fresh *tls.Config.

symbols.name: Load
symbols.doc:
Load reads the named TLS material from disk and returns the opaque identity.
A configured-but-unreadable file is an error, never a silently skipped one.

symbols.name: MaterialInvalid

code.public: The TLS material is missing or invalid

symbols.doc:
MaterialInvalid reports TLS material that is missing, unreadable,
malformed, or that yields no usable certificate. It is never downgraded to
an empty trust store.

symbols.name: New
symbols.doc:
New validates TLS material held in memory and returns the opaque identity. It
applies exactly the same rules as Load; only the source of the bytes differs.

symbols.name: Params
symbols.doc: Params carries TLS material already held in memory.

symbols.name: AcceptKey
symbols.doc:
AcceptKey computes the Sec-WebSocket-Accept value for a client's
Sec-WebSocket-Key (RFC 6455 §4.2.2).

It is exported for tests and for anyone writing a client handshake by hand.
The digest is SHA-1 by the RFC's own instruction and is not a security
primitive: its job is to prove the server parsed the handshake rather than
replaying it, so a cached 101 cannot pass for a live upgrade.

symbols.name: AllowAnyOrigin
symbols.doc:
AllowAnyOrigin disables the origin check.

It has to be written out because the browser's same-origin policy does not
apply to WebSocket: any page may open a connection to this server and the
browser will attach the user's cookies to the handshake. Reach for it when
authentication does not ride on ambient credentials — a bearer token, a
signed ticket — which is exactly when the origin proves nothing anyway.

symbols.name: AllowOrigins
symbols.doc:
AllowOrigins replaces the default same-origin rule with an exact allowlist.

The comparison is on the whole Origin header — scheme, host and port —
case-insensitively. Matching the host alone would accept http:// for an https
server, which is the downgrade the check exists to notice. Behind a proxy
that terminates TLS this is the only way to have the scheme checked at all:
the request arrives in plaintext there, so the default rule cannot see which
scheme the browser used.

symbols.name: CloseAbnormal
symbols.doc: CloseAbnormal means the connection died without a Close frame.

symbols.name: CloseCode
symbols.doc: CloseCode is the status code a Close frame carries (RFC 6455 §7.4).

symbols.name: CloseExtensionRequired
symbols.doc: CloseExtensionRequired is a client giving up for want of an extension.

symbols.name: CloseGoingAway
symbols.doc: CloseGoingAway is a server shutting down; it is what a drain sends.

symbols.name: CloseInternalError
symbols.doc: CloseInternalError is an unexpected condition on this side.

symbols.name: CloseInvalidPayload
symbols.doc: CloseInvalidPayload is text that is not valid UTF-8.

symbols.name: CloseNoStatus
symbols.doc: CloseNoStatus means the peer's Close frame carried no code.

symbols.name: CloseNormal
symbols.doc: CloseNormal is a completed purpose, on either side.

symbols.name: ClosePolicyViolation
symbols.doc: ClosePolicyViolation is the generic refusal when no other code fits.

symbols.name: CloseProtocolError
symbols.doc: CloseProtocolError is a frame the RFC forbids.

symbols.name: CloseTLSHandshake
symbols.doc: CloseTLSHandshake means the TLS handshake failed.

symbols.name: CloseTooLarge
symbols.doc: CloseTooLarge is a message beyond what this endpoint accepts.

symbols.name: CloseUnsupportedData
symbols.doc:
CloseUnsupportedData is a well-formed frame carrying data this endpoint
cannot accept.

symbols.name: Conn
symbols.doc:
Conn is one upgraded WebSocket connection.

Exactly one goroutine loops on [Conn].Receive for the connection's whole
life. Never two: the protocol is a single ordered frame stream, so two
readers would each take half of a message. Never zero: that loop is also
where Pings are answered, where the peer's Close is replied to and where the
heartbeat sees the peer alive, so a connection nobody reads is ended within
two ping intervals — see the package documentation for the push-handler
shape. Writes are safe for concurrent use.

symbols.name: ConnClosed

code.public: The WebSocket connection is closed

symbols.doc:
ConnClosed reports an operation on a connection that has ended. It is the
terminal outcome a receive loop runs until, and it carries the peer's
close code when there was one.

symbols.name: ConnMisconfigured

code.public: The WebSocket options are not valid

symbols.doc:
ConnMisconfigured reports an option the domain refuses to interpret
rather than guess at, such as a negative ping interval.

symbols.name: DefaultMaxFrameSize
symbols.doc: DefaultMaxFrameSize is the ceiling on a single frame's announced payload.

symbols.name: DefaultMaxMessageSize
symbols.doc: DefaultMaxMessageSize is the ceiling on one reassembled message.

symbols.name: DefaultPingInterval
symbols.doc:
DefaultPingInterval is the heartbeat cadence a connection uses when the
caller sets none. It sits under the idle timeout of every proxy worth naming.

symbols.name: DefaultWriteTimeout
symbols.doc:
DefaultWriteTimeout bounds ONE frame's write. A connection has no total write
budget by nature; this is what stops a peer that has stopped reading from
pinning a goroutine forever.

symbols.name: DrainSignal
symbols.doc:
DrainSignal returns the channel closed when the server serving this request
begins draining, or nil when it publishes none.

[Conn] watches it for you. It is re-exported here because a handler often
wants to stop its own work at the same moment, and a nil channel blocks
forever, so a select that watches it needs no nil check.

symbols.name: GUID
symbols.doc:
GUID is the fixed string RFC 6455 §1.3 concatenates to the client's key
before hashing. It is a constant of the protocol, not a secret.

symbols.name: HandshakeFailed

code.public: The WebSocket handshake is not valid

symbols.doc:
HandshakeFailed reports a request that is not a valid RFC 6455 opening
handshake, or one whose origin the policy refused. [Upgrade] has already
written the HTTP response when it returns this.

symbols.name: InvalidPayload

code.public: The WebSocket payload is not valid

symbols.doc:
InvalidPayload reports text that is not UTF-8, a close code that must
never travel, or a close reason past the control-frame ceiling.

symbols.name: MaxControlPayload
symbols.doc:
MaxControlPayload is the ceiling RFC 6455 §5.5 puts on a control frame's
payload, and therefore on a [Conn].Ping payload or a close reason.

symbols.name: MaxFrameSize
symbols.doc:
MaxFrameSize bounds one frame's ANNOUNCED payload length.

It is separate from [MaxMessageSize] because it is enforced at a different
moment: against the header, before a byte is read or allocated. A ceiling
above the message ceiling can never be reached and is refused as a mistake.

symbols.name: MaxMessageSize
symbols.doc:
MaxMessageSize bounds one reassembled message.

Zero is clamped to [DefaultMaxMessageSize], negative is refused. There is
deliberately no "unbounded" setting: the length is announced by the peer in a
64-bit field, and fragmentation lets it keep announcing more, so an unbounded
ceiling is not a configuration choice — it is a remote memory allocator.

symbols.name: Message
symbols.doc: Message is one complete WebSocket application message.

symbols.name: MessageTooLarge

code.public: The WebSocket message is larger than the accepted size

symbols.doc:
MessageTooLarge reports a frame or a reassembled message beyond the
configured ceiling, refused before any buffer was sized from it.

symbols.name: Option
symbols.doc: Option configures a Conn.

symbols.name: PingInterval
symbols.doc:
PingInterval sets how often the connection pings an otherwise silent peer.

Zero does not mean "never": it is clamped to [DefaultPingInterval], because a
connection with the heartbeat silently disabled works perfectly on loopback
and then stops noticing peers that vanish — which is how a mobile client
normally leaves. A negative interval is refused; "never" is [WithoutPing].

The heartbeat counts frames the handler has READ, so it keeps a connection
open only while one goroutine loops on [Conn].Receive; a connection nobody
reads is ended within two intervals, however healthy the peer.

symbols.name: ProtocolViolation

code.public: The WebSocket frame is not valid

symbols.doc:
ProtocolViolation reports a frame RFC 6455 forbids. The connection has
already been failed when it surfaces.

symbols.name: Subprotocols
symbols.doc:
Subprotocols declares the subprotocols this server speaks, most preferred
first.

The SERVER's order decides. A client advertises what it can speak; choosing
among those is the server's call, or a client that listed a deprecated
dialect first could pin the server to it forever. No overlap is not a failure
— the upgrade succeeds with no subprotocol, which RFC 6455 §4.2.2 names as
the way to say "none agreed".

Each name must be an RFC 7230 token, since the chosen one is written into
the response verbatim; a name with a space, a comma or a quote is refused at
Upgrade. The list is copied, so reusing the slice changes nothing later.

symbols.name: Upgrade
symbols.spelled: func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, opts ...Option) (conn *Conn, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(w net/http.ResponseWriter, r *net/http.Request, opts ...github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/websocket.Option) (conn *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/net/websocket.Conn, err error)
symbols.doc:
Upgrade completes the RFC 6455 opening handshake and returns the connection.

On failure it has ALREADY written the HTTP response — a 426 carrying the
version this server speaks, a 400, a 403 or a 405 as the fault requires — so
the handler should simply return.

The socket is taken over from net/http. It is no longer the HTTP server's to
close, nor this SDK's listener engine's: it is the handler's until
[Conn].Close.

symbols.name: UpgradeUnsupported

code.public: The connection cannot be upgraded

symbols.doc:
UpgradeUnsupported reports a response whose connection cannot be taken
over — HTTP/2, or a middleware that wraps the ResponseWriter without
forwarding Unwrap. The request was fine; this stack cannot serve it.

symbols.name: Version
symbols.doc:
Version is the only protocol version this server speaks. A request naming
another is refused WITH this value advertised back, so a client can
renegotiate instead of guessing.

symbols.name: WithoutPing
symbols.doc:
WithoutPing disables the heartbeat, and with it the connection's only
liveness check. Use it where the transport provides its own.

symbols.name: WriteTimeout
symbols.doc:
WriteTimeout bounds how long one frame's write may take.

It is per-frame on purpose: a group's WriteTimeout is an absolute deadline
for one HTTP response, and this connection outlives the response entirely.
Zero is clamped to [DefaultWriteTimeout], negative is refused.
